output.summary: DRUG REVIEW — TRIPTANS IN HEMIPLEGIC MIGRAINE FINDINGS: Triptans (5-HT1B/1D agonists) exert vasoconstrictive effects on cerebral and meningeal vasculature. In the context of hemiplegic migraine — where motor aura is associated with cortical spreading depression and haemodynamic changes — most international guidelines caution against triptan use during motor aura episodes due to theoretical vasoconstrictive risk, although the evidence base is limited. CATEGORY: Triptans are cautioned (not universally absolutely contraindicated) in hemiplegic migraine; individual guideline recommendations vary. Clinical correlation recommended. Triptans are cautioned in hemiplegic migraine due to theoretical vasoconstrictive risk during motor aura; category-level caution applies;

patient.history_present_illness:
A 39-year-old Japanese man with a long-standing history of myofascial pain syndrome and intermittent headaches was referred to the neurology outpatient clinic for urgent evaluation after two episodes of transient right-sided limb weakness. The first episode occurred 20 days prior to this visit: he noticed weakness in his right arm and right leg while at home, along with a tense, numb feeling on the right side of his face. These symptoms developed gradually over approximately 20-25 minutes and resolved over the following 30-40 minutes. Afterwards, he experienced a left occipital headache that he treated with loxoprofen with good relief.

The second episode occurred 2 days before this visit. He was at work when he again developed right upper and lower limb weakness and a tense feeling on the left side of his mouth. He was found unresponsive by a colleague and transported by ambulance to a local emergency department. En route to hospital, he regained consciousness and complained of a left occipital headache. At the emergency department, he was alert with right limb weakness and sensory disturbance over the ulnar aspect of the right upper arm. He was admitted for observation. His symptoms gradually improved over several hours and he was discharged with an outpatient referral when no acute cause was identified.

He has a history of migraine headaches and myofascial pain, managed with lomerizine hydrochloride and as-needed NSAIDs. He has no prior stroke, no hypertension, no diabetes, and no cardiac disease. He is a non-smoker. He reports no family history of hemiplegic migraine. He is now headache-free and fully neurologically intact at this consultation.
